reviews.text:
I took my elderly parakeet to the vet because it was unwell and losing weight.
During the examination, I received a brief explanation of the basic tests and how to manage the weight loss. However, there was no explanation of the cause of the weight loss, nor was there any discussion of additional tests considering the bird's age, possible illnesses, or guidelines for future monitoring.
A few months later, my beloved bird died from kidney disease.
Looking back, I realize I should have investigated further myself. However, at the time, there were no other major abnormalities besides the weight loss, and the vet only explained how to help the bird gain weight, so I didn't think it was that serious.
I'm not saying that it could have been saved if tests had been done, but if I had received an explanation about the possibility of illness and future risks, I think I could have considered additional tests or a second opinion.
Precisely because it was a hospital known for treating birds, I wish they had explained not only the diagnosis but also the possible causes of the weight loss and the available treatment options.

My one-year-old degu had trouble using its front leg, so I took it in for an examination. The doctor examined it thoroughly and explained everything clearly.

It was diagnosed as a sprain and prescribed medication. I have a follow-up appointment in a week. They also discussed various ways to administer the medication and helped me decide on the best approach.

I mixed the liquid medicine with its favorite treat, and it ate it without any problems!

I was worried, but bringing it to this hospital was definitely the right decision.

My pet cat has been a patient here for over 15 years, ever since the previous director took over.

Even after the change to the current director, the clear explanations and meticulous care remain unchanged, and I feel reassured knowing they'll answer calls outside of regular hours in emergencies.

They're open almost year-round (closed only on Sunday and public holiday afternoons), so I sometimes worry about when the doctors actually get any rest.
The teacher is very friendly and easy to talk to!

I always have my Java Sparrow examined here.
No appointment is necessary (although I do call in advance), and if there are any symptoms they are seen quickly and the diagnosis is accurate.
I also use their hotel when I travel.
The doctors and staff are truly trustworthy!
I had my hamster treated there. They were thorough and trustworthy.
The teacher was very kind and explained everything very carefully.

Thank you for your continued support! We have our chickens looked after by you, and you are very experienced. Your assistants are friendly, efficient, and you can feel their love for animals... You also take good care of dogs and other animals, so we will definitely come here if anything comes up.

There may be various reviews, but I have nothing but gratitude for the doctors and staff here. If you're worried that your dog, cat, bird, or any other animal won't get better and don't know what to do, I recommend you come here at least once. It will definitely save your life and your feelings. In short, there is no better hospital out there!! It's truly amazing!!

I'm taking my sugar glider there for treatment. The vet is very thorough, explains things clearly, and is very kind. I often see small birds there as well, so I feel they are stronger in treating exotic animals compared to other clinics. Also, since the veterinarian directly manages the animals, I feel relatively safe using it as a pet hotel. I've had treatment there several times, and the prices aren't too high.
It's helpful that they're open on weekends and late at night.

I recently lost my Richardson's ground squirrel at this hospital. It was a short life, only 2 years and 8 months old.

I received a call 30 minutes before my scheduled pickup time, saying it had suffered a seizure due to dehydration and I needed to come immediately. I was at my own hospital, but I left early and arrived 15 minutes later, only to find that they were already performing CPR and it was no longer breathing.

It was true that it was weak and had no appetite, but just the day before it had been running around and showing signs of life. I couldn't accept its sudden death, and I cried uncontrollably, regardless of who was watching, and the tears wouldn't stop on the way home.

Even after returning home, the shock and tears wouldn't stop; I felt like I was going crazy. My family and I cried even more when we got home, and even now, I can't come to terms with it. I feel overwhelmed by the magnitude of my own guilt for not being able to save it.

The reason I'm posting here is because I still have doubts about its sudden death.

My husband also said it's impossible for a ground squirrel that was so energetic to suffer a seizure from dehydration. He said it's natural for it to be dehydrated, since blood had been drawn for a blood test. The question arose: if the doctor knew what was happening, why didn't they administer fluid injections or IV fluids sooner?

On the day of the visit, the head veterinarian explained that the dog was dehydrated, wasn't urinating much, had high blood sugar, and then suddenly had a seizure in the evening. The only charge was for the blood test. However, the shock of death was so great that I couldn't think clearly enough to question the hospital's treatment.

But, after a few days, the more I thought about my dog's death, the more I couldn't accept it as inevitable. Looking back now, I think what my family said made more sense. I feel like this life could have been saved, that she suffered from dehydration at the end and was neglected in a corner of the hospital. I have nowhere to go with these feelings, so I decided to post here.

Originally, at the beginning of October, her weight was 400 grams, but it dropped to around 350 grams in just a few days. Even considering it was her estrus period, I felt something was wrong, so I took her to this hospital, where we usually take her for sprains, tooth trimming, and pet boarding.

Initially, the diagnosis was unknown, and we tried trimming its teeth. There was no improvement, so it was prescribed oral medication to stimulate its appetite. However, after several days of giving it the medication, it didn't recover, so we went back to the vet. They suspected it might be a kidney or liver problem and prescribed medication again, but it still didn't improve. After another vet visit, and a full day of blood tests, it was finally diagnosed with congenital diabetes two weeks later, after four visits. By this time, its weight had dropped to about 280 grams.

Until then, to prevent obesity, we had been feeding it Richardson's ground squirrel-specific pellets, timothy hay, a small amount of sunflower seeds, and occasionally vegetables and fruits. Now, however, we were simply told to feed it anything it would eat. We tried giving it rabbit pellets once, as suggested, but since it had stopped eating its regular pellets, it naturally refused the rabbit pellets as well.

I didn't know how to feed it, so I tried various methods I learned from online searches. I cut the food into small pieces, softened and chopped pellets, and even mashed up things like bananas like baby food and put them on a plate. At first, it would eat most of it, but by the next morning it was all dried up and shriveled. Towards the end, I had tried everything, and I was at a loss as to what to give it. I even tried giving it tofu and whitebait. However, it wouldn't eat anything, and it rapidly weakened, becoming emaciated and losing weight again, down to about 260 grams.

Even then, all I was given was the next dose of medication, and I was only told that it probably wanted to eat but wouldn't because it felt nauseous.

I knew that there were few hospitals that could treat Richardson's ground squirrels, and that it was a difficult animal to treat because there were few cases.

However, this hospital seemed to cover almost all exotic animals and had extensive knowledge. They explained the illness carefully to me and other patients, so I had complete trust in them, including based on word of mouth.

So I did as I was told, and took him to the hospital on the designated days as instructed.
However, no matter how many times I changed his medication, his appetite didn't recover. Eventually, he refused to take it, spitting it out. He wouldn't eat much of anything I offered, and his weight kept decreasing. Despite numerous consultations, I received no specific guidance regarding his diet at home.
Looking back now, I've researched various options and found posts from hospitals suggesting that these types of squirrels recover more easily if they are given a liquid diet of nutritious food mixed with yogurt, force-fed several times a day using a dropper.
Furthermore, it was mentioned that Richardson's ground squirrels with diabetes are prone to dehydration, so care should be taken to prevent dehydration. A drop in body temperature also weakens metabolic capacity, so the room temperature should be set higher than the ideal temperature. They are also prone to stress, so care should be taken during hospital visits.
Of course, I received no guidance on any of this.
Looking back, even in the eight days leading up to his death, I was urged to take him to the hospital four times, and blood tests were performed each time.

Even for a human, it's painful to imagine, so imagine how stressful and difficult this treatment must have been for the Richardson's ground squirrel, which is prone to accumulating stress.

Even though it was to check the effects of the oral medication and measure blood sugar levels, couldn't there have been other guidance or methods to help with the deteriorating physical condition as the squirrel lost 5-10 grams of blood sugar each day?

I grew up in an environment where animals were a normal part of life, and I've kept many different kinds of animals, mainly dogs, cats, and birds. So I think I was overconfident somewhere along the way.

I regret that I made excuses about the busyness of my daily work, and that I relied entirely on the vet because of the unfamiliar difficulties of caring for an exotic animal. I neglected to research more about veterinary diabetes and treatments myself, and that I didn't suggest other treatment options.

I also regret that there might have been more I could have done, and that I shouldn't have taken that squirrel, who had become even weaker after refusing to take the medication, to the vet that day just because I was told to.

Furthermore, I had taken my child to the vet before picking up the kitten, but despite having an appointment, a mistake at the hospital made me wait for over 30 minutes. Since I then had to go to my own hospital appointment, I couldn't pick up the kitten earlier, which in hindsight feels like a series of unfortunate events.

If that appointment mistake hadn't happened, and I had picked up the kitten more than 30 minutes earlier, I could have requested a hydration injection myself, and I might have been able to prevent dehydration by feeding it at home. I might even have been able to be there for its final moments.

Certainly, I think the kitten's death that day was partly due to these unfortunate circumstances.

However, although the kitten was weak, I believe it could have lived much longer with proper treatment.

At the end, it was a very small kitten, weighing only about 250 grams. Even so, its behavior and personality were incredibly endearing; everything it did was comforting, and it was a very, very important presence in our family.

Therefore, the sense of loss is immense, and the weight of this kitten's life still weighs heavily on me.

Every single day since then, I've thought about this little one, crying until my eyes were swollen, and there were days when I couldn't sleep and the night passed.

For the past 25 years, since leaving home and starting my own family, I've never owned a pet because I understood the responsibility that comes with it. This was my children's first pet as well. I feel so guilty and lost that I can't recover from the way this special little one met their end.

It was my first pet in a long time, and my family's first pet, but we've now talked about never owning another pet again.

Of course, I believe the hospital staff acted with the best interests of this little one in mind regarding treatment. They even cried with us at the end.

However, I don't believe they did their absolute best during that half-day.

Of course, animals are part of the family.

I hope that those working in animal medicine will reaffirm that even a small misjudgment can be life-threatening because of their small size, that this can lead to a family like ours, and that the value of a life is just as great as a human life.

Thank you for everything.

I took my budgie to the vet. They were very accommodating and provided excellent service, even outside of regular hours.

There's another bird specialist vet nearby, but it's more profit-driven, so I'm glad I switched to this one.

My 19-year-old Mississippi map turtle stopped eating, so I took him in for treatment.
There aren't many hospitals that will treat turtles, so this was a big help.
After giving him medication, he was fully cured in two weeks!
By the way, I was prepared for the consultation and medication to cost tens of thousands of yen, but it was only a little under 10,000 yen, so I was very grateful.
Thank you for your continued support!

I am grateful for the care I receive at the hotel and medical clinic. The doctors and staff are all really nice people, and I can really feel their love for the animals. Thank you for always treating me so kindly.

I took my chameleon in for an examination. The doctor explained everything in great detail and was a really good vet. I would recommend this place to everyone around me, and I won't go anywhere else anymore! It was a really good hospital.

The teachers and assistants are very kind and I like them.
They answer my questions carefully, so I feel at ease and can leave my child in their care.
